lesson.title: When a Limit Runs Off to Infinity
lesson.summary: Sometimes a function does not settle near any finite number as x approaches a value, it grows without bound instead, and infinite limit notation gives that runaway behavior a precise, useful description.
lesson.body:
The basic definition of a limit requires a function's outputs to get arbitrarily close to some specific, finite number L. Certain functions near certain x-values never do that: their outputs instead grow larger and larger, or more and more negative, without settling near any single number at all. This behavior is described using infinite limit notation, lim as x approaches a of f(x) equals infinity, or equals negative infinity, with the understanding that infinity is not a number the function actually reaches. It is a description of unbounded growth, so strictly speaking the limit still fails to exist as a finite value; the infinite notation simply describes how it fails to exist, which is more informative than saying nothing at all.

Worked example 1: find lim as x approaches 0 of 1/x^2. As x approaches 0 from either direction, x^2 becomes a tiny positive number (since squaring removes any sign), so 1/x^2 becomes an enormous positive number, and this happens identically whether x approaches from the left or the right, because (-0.1)^2 equals 0.01 just as (0.1)^2 does. A table confirms this: at x = 0.1, 1/x^2 = 1/0.01 = 100. At x = 0.01, 1/x^2 = 1/0.0001 = 10,000. At x = 0.001, 1/x^2 = 1/0.000001 = 1,000,000. Both sides diverge to positive infinity, so lim as x approaches 0 of 1/x^2 equals infinity, a genuine two-sided infinite limit, and the graph of 1/x^2 has a vertical asymptote at x = 0.

Worked example 2 shows a case where the two one-sided behaviors disagree: find the behavior of 1/x as x approaches 0. From the right, x is small and positive, so 1/x is large and positive, heading toward positive infinity. From the left, x is small and negative, so 1/x is large and negative, heading toward negative infinity. Because the right side heads to positive infinity while the left side heads to negative infinity, these two behaviors do not match, so the full two-sided limit, lim as x approaches 0 of 1/x, does not exist, not even as an infinite limit. Only the one-sided limits can honestly be labeled infinite here: lim as x approaches 0 from the right of 1/x equals infinity, and lim as x approaches 0 from the left of 1/x equals negative infinity.

Every infinite limit corresponds to a vertical asymptote on the function's graph, connecting directly back to limits-from-graphs: wherever lim as x approaches a of f(x) is infinite, from one side or both, the curve hugs the vertical line x = a ever more tightly but never crosses it. This is common in rational functions whenever a particular x-value makes the denominator equal 0 without also making the numerator equal 0, which is the opposite situation from the removable holes seen earlier in complex fractions and limits-from-tables, where numerator and denominator share a common zero and cancel instead of blowing up.

It is worth keeping infinite limits distinct from a related but different idea, limits at infinity. Infinite limits describe what a function does near one specific, finite input value, producing a vertical asymptote there. Limits at infinity instead describe what a function does as the input itself grows without bound, describing horizontal end behavior far out along the x-axis. Both use the word infinity, but they answer different questions about a function's graph.
